# Reproduction of RL Training for Heterogeneous Robots with UniLab + MotrixSim

This chapter shows you how to run the UniLab MotrixSim backend and PPO training process successfully on a Windows laptop with 6GB of memory. The main focus of this experiment is robot state-based RL: the policy network reads the robot state, velocity commands, and historical observations, samples during CPU-side simulation, and then updates parameters via the GPU learner. Rendering is not the core method of this chapter; it serves only as a supplementary step for checkpoint verification, result display, and an experience of MotrixSim PBR.

The machine used in this test is an RTX 3060 Laptop 6GB, AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, with 64GB of memory. Finally, `go2_joystick_flat + motrix + ppo` was successfully implemented. The maximum tested configuration consists of `512` parallel environments and `100` training iterations, totaling `1,228,800` environment steps.

## 1. What problem does UniLab solve

The core idea of UniLab is to divide robot RL training into two parts: the CPU side handles large-scale physical simulation and data collection, while the GPU side is responsible for policy network learning. The significance of this approach is that it does not require a GPU-based physical simulator to start large-scale robot RL; as long as the CPU can parallelly process enough environments, the GPU only needs to handle the learning tasks.

Figure 1: Official system architecture diagram of UniLab. Pay special attention to the Runtime Flow Spine in the middle: CPU Workers handle MuJoCo/MotrixSim simulation, Host IPC manages shared memory, rollout, and replay buffer, while Device Learner is the learning module for CUDA / Apple / AMD / Intel devices. Source: [ Official UniLab project page ](https://unilabsim.github.io).

## 2. To what extent can this chapter be reproduced

This 6GB GPU can handle small-scale training, but it is not recommended as a complete paper reproduction platform. There are two reasons for this: first, the 3-10x end-to-end efficiency improvements mentioned in the papers require comparisons across multiple tasks, algorithms, and hardware configurations; second, the official platform currently supports Linux CUDA, Linux ROCm, Linux XPU, and macOS, while Windows is not part of the official support scope.

The conclusions obtained in this chapter are more suitable for beginners to make judgments:

| Item | Current Status of This Chapter |
| --- | --- |
| Clone of UniLab Official Repository | Completed |
| Import of MotrixSim Backend | Completed |
| CUDA Version of PyTorch | Completed, `torch 2.7.0+cu128` |
| `go2_joystick_flat` Training | Completed |
| Checkpoint Saving | Completed |
| No rendering eval | Completed |
| MotrixSim Record Video | Completed |
| MuJoCo Backend | Not working on Windows, stuck at `mujoco-uni` build |
| Complete Paper Benchmark | Not reproduced, requires Linux/cloud server and a more systematic experimental matrix |

## 3. Environment Preparation

The official recommendation is to use `uv` for the management environment. This machine already has a `micromamba` `py310` environment, so no new micromamba environment is created here. Instead, UniLab creates its own `.venv` in the project directory. This approach isolates UniLab dependencies and does not contaminate the existing environment.

First, write the working directory and repository path as variables:

```powershell
$WORKSPACE = "C:\path\to\workspace"
$UNILAB_ROOT = "$WORKSPACE\UniLab"
git clone https://github.com/unilabsim/UniLab.git $UNILAB_ROOT
cd $UNILAB_ROOT
```

If you want to reproduce it on Linux, use the official command first:

```bash
make setup-motrix
```

When running this machine with Windows, there is no available Windows wheel for `mujoco-uni==3.8.0`. Source build requires `MUJOCO_PATH`. To first run the MotrixSim route successfully, the following compromise command is used to skip `mujoco-uni`:

```powershell
uv sync --extra motrix --no-install-package mujoco-uni `
  --python C:\path\to\micromamba\envs\py310\python.exe
```

Then replace PyTorch in the project `.venv` with the Windows CUDA 12.8 wheel:

```powershell
uv pip install --python .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe --reinstall `
  torch==2.7.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
```

Check if CUDA is available:

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
uv run --no-sync python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available()); print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))"
```

Output of this machine:

```text
2.7.0+cu128 12.8 True
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU
```

## 4. Checkpoint 1: Run a small-scale training in the 256 environment first

For the first time, it is recommended not to directly use the official default `1024` environment. On a machine with 6GB of VRAM, start with `256` environment to ensure that the training loop, logs, and checkpoints function properly.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
$env:WANDB_MODE = "disabled"

uv run --no-sync train --algo ppo --task go2_joystick_flat --sim motrix `
  training.no_play=true training.device=cuda:0 `
  algo.num_envs=256 algo.max_iterations=50 algo.save_interval=50
```

This command does three things: it uses MotrixSim on the CPU to advance the Go2 flat terrain tracking task; it updates the policy using the PPO learner on CUDA; and it saves a checkpoint every 50 iterations. `training.no_play=true` will turn off the post-training interactive replay to avoid window rendering from affecting training and validation.

The summary of this machine's successful training in one attempt is as follows:

| Metric | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Number of parallel environments | 256 |
| Iteration | 50 |
| `num_steps_per_env` | 24 |
| Cumulative environment steps | 307,200 |
| Training wall time | 51.30 s |
| Final mean reward | 22.48 |
| Best mean reward | 25.52 |
| Final checkpoint | `model_49.pt` |

This smoke test demonstrates that data collection, GPU learner, log writing, and checkpoint saving all work properly; however, it cannot prove that the policy has reached the level required by papers or official benchmarks.

## 5. Checkpoint 2: Resource usage in 512 environment, 100 iterations

After confirming that the 256 environment can run, this machine continued to run `512` environments and `100` iterations, and performed coarse-grained monitoring using `nvidia-smi`, Windows counter, and process RSS.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
$env:WANDB_MODE = "disabled"

uv run --no-sync train --algo ppo --task go2_joystick_flat --sim motrix `
  training.no_play=true training.device=cuda:0 `
  algo.num_envs=512 algo.max_iterations=100 algo.save_interval=50
```

Training Summary:

| Metric | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Number of parallel environments | 512 |
| Iteration | 100 |
| Cumulative environment steps | 1,228,800 |
| Training wall time | 132.90 s |
| Outer monitoring record duration | 141.94 s |
| Final mean reward | 34.97 |
| Best mean reward | 37.40 |
| Average episode length | 1000.0 |

Resource usage records:

| Resource Item | Average Value | Peak Value | Explanation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| GPU Memory | 233 MiB | 263 MiB | Contains only `nvidia-smi` sample values, indicating that the policy network is lightweight |
| GPU Utilization | 13.54% | 60% | The learner updates intermittently, so utilization does not reach 100% for long periods |
| System CPU Usage | 62.80% | 81.05% | MotrixSim/CPU parallel simulation is the main load |
| Used System Memory | 31.22 GiB | 32.24 GiB | Includes the system and background processes; not exclusive to UniLab |
| UniLab-related Python RSS | 1397 MiB | 1538 MiB | Estimated from the working set of related Python/uv processes |

The monitoring file is saved in:

- `assets/local_runs/20260531-210237/resource_monitor.csv`
- `assets/local_runs/20260531-210237/resource_summary_512x100.json`
- `assets/local_runs/20260531-210237/train_summary_512x100.json`

From this set of data, it can be seen that the 6GB graphics card is not the bottleneck for this lightweight task; the CPU is the more obvious source of pressure. This also aligns with the design of UniLab: the CPU handles the physical simulation, while the GPU is used only for policy learning.

## 6. Checkpoint 3: Export MotrixSim training replay

In Windows, if the repository path contains Chinese characters, `eval --render-mode record` may produce an error when exporting the TorchScript policy:

```text
RuntimeError: Parent directory ... does not exist.
```

The issue with this machine is that the original path contains Chinese characters, and TorchScript does not handle this path correctly during saving. The solution is to place the root directory of the training logs in an ASCII path, such as `C:/unilab_logs`.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
$env:WANDB_MODE = "disabled"

uv run --no-sync train --algo ppo --task go2_joystick_flat --sim motrix `
  training.no_play=true training.device=cuda:0 training.log_root=C:/unilab_logs `
  algo.num_envs=256 algo.max_iterations=50 algo.save_interval=50
```

The policy exported here is the policy replay of the training-후 checkpoint, not a PBR teaser. Its purpose is to verify that the state-based policy can be loaded and can advance several steps smoothly in MotrixSim.

Multi-environment replay:

```powershell
uv run --no-sync eval --algo ppo --task go2_joystick_flat --sim motrix `
  --load-run -1 --render-mode record `
  training.log_root=C:/unilab_logs `
  training.play_steps=300 training.play_env_num=4 training.render_spacing=1.4
```

Single environment follow perspective replay:

```powershell
uv run --no-sync eval --algo ppo --task go2_joystick_flat --sim motrix `
  --load-run -1 --render-mode record `
  training.log_root=C:/unilab_logs `
  training.play_steps=300 training.play_env_num=1 `
  training.cam_tracking=true training.cam_distance=4.0 training.cam_elevation=-15.0
```

## 7. Extended Experience: MotrixSim PBR teaser renderer

The focus of UniLab’s work line is not on creating rendering benchmarks, but the MotrixSim renderer already supports PBR. The official repository provides an independent teaser entry that can be used as a visual experience tutorial: it loads the paper teaser scene, activates the MotrixSim renderer, and maintains a static scene display; it does not train policies nor advance the RL rollout.

Run in the root directory of the UniLab repository:

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
uv run --no-sync demo teaser
```

The first run will automatically download the teaser scene assets. After the download is complete, the program will enter `src/unilab/tools/render_teaser.py`, call `RenderSettings.quality()`, and enable shadow, SSGI, and full render mesh. After the window opens, you can interact with the scene through the renderer; close the window to exit.

To stabilize the extraction of multi-view images, this machine uses MotrixSim's headless system camera capture instead of recording chat videos or capturing front windows. The core approach is to load the same teaser MJCF scene and then adjust it multiple times:

```python
render.system_camera.set_view(lookat, distance, elevation, azimuth)
```

After the scene assets are downloaded, this machine exports 3 `1280x720` PNG screenshots, using approximately `24 s`. The first run will additionally download `scenes/teaser` assets. If warnings such as `convex hull partial success`, `Duplicate AssetLoader`, or `wgpu_core::validation` appear in the log, as long as the screenshots are generated correctly, they can generally be treated as a prompt for the renderer initialization.

The three images below are all from the MotrixSim PBR renderer running on this machine.

## 8. Common Issues

### Build failed for `mujoco-uni` under Windows

The error message of this machine is:

```text
RuntimeError: MUJOCO_PATH environment variable is not set, and no bundled MuJoCo found in package.
```

This is a limitation of the Windows approach, but it does not mean that UniLab itself cannot be used. If you want to seriously reproduce the MuJoCo backend and the corresponding paper experiments, it is recommended to use Linux CUDA or Docker; if you just want to run MotrixSim first, you can skip `mujoco-uni` as described in this chapter.

### `unilab` Package import failed

This machine has encountered a situation under Windows where `uv run train` is found, but `unilab` cannot be found. The solution is to explicitly set it in the current PowerShell session:

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
```

### Error when exporting video to a path containing Chinese characters

Place the training logs and checkpoints under an ASCII path:

```powershell
training.log_root=C:/unilab_logs
```

This is more stable than moving the entire project, and it won't damage the tutorial repository structure.

### Can a 6GB GPU continue to support more environments?

For this task in this chapter, the 512 environment does not utilize all 6GB of VRAM. The bottleneck lies more in simulation and scheduling on the CPU side. You can continue to try `algo.num_envs=768` or `1024`, but it is recommended to modify only one parameter at a time while keeping `training.no_play=true`. If the CPU utilization remains very high and the training speed decreases instead of improving, it indicates that the number of environments has exceeded the effective parallel capacity of this machine.

## 9. Conclusion of this chapter

This 6GB RTX 3060 laptop can run UniLab’s lightweight state-based RL training through the MotrixSim route on Windows. The most valuable result is not the reward values, but the confirmation that UniLab’s heterogeneous design works well on small machines: the CPU handles parallel simulation, the GPU handles policy learning, with very low VRAM usage, and the CPU is the main resource bottleneck.

If you want to reproduce the complete paper, it is recommended to switch to the Linux CUDA environment and use the officially supported `make setup-motrix` approach. Additionally, ensure the MuJoCo backend, multi-task, multi-algorithm, and multi-hardware comparisons are included. A 6GB GPU is more suitable as a platform for course smoke tests, environment validation, and small-scale ablation experiments.
